quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A stop consonant squeezed between two other consonants rarely survives in fast speech. Listen for the /t/ in "strict diet" — is it there?
quests.explanation: Consonant clusters like this one are common at word boundaries in English, and the middle stop is almost always the casualty. The /t/ drops out of "strict diet" for exactly that reason.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's no /j/ anywhere in the spelling of "agree". Yet something links it to the vowel that opens "about" — what is it?
quests.explanation: This inserted /j/ has no basis in spelling — it exists purely to smooth the vowel-to-vowel transition between "agree" and "about". That's the hallmark of intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "that" to "pen". Is it still /t/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /t/ meets a bilabial sound, the /t/ shifts to /p/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "that pen".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "ground floor" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /d/ in "ground" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /d/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "ground floor", the /d/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "great" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the bilabial sound in "match"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a bilabial position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /p/ in "great match".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "backyard" and "party". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /d/ in "backyard party" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "hot". With a bilabial consonant starting "bath" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /t/ ending "hot" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /t/ becomes /p/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "bath".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /t/ at the end of "taste". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "good"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /t/ at the end of "taste" disappears before the consonant that starts "good".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen carefully between "law" and "and". An unwritten sound appears purely to ease the vowel-to-vowel transition. Which one?
quests.explanation: Native speakers automatically fill the gap between two vowel sounds with /r/, even when there's no letter to justify it. "law and" is a clear example of this intrusive sound.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "bad meal" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /d/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /d/ rarely stays /d/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /b/, which is exactly what you hear in "bad meal".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.explanation: Since "blue" doesn't end in a written consonant that could explain a /w/, the /w/ you hear before "eyes" is added by the speech system itself — an intrusive sound, not a spelled one.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Nothing in "yoga"'s ending suggests a consonant at all. So the /r/ you might hear before "is" isn't really part of either word — where does it come from?

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "across your" quickly and casually. The /s/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /s/ and /j/ into /ʃ/. That's why "across your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "crew" has no letter for /w/ anywhere at its end. So if you hear a /w/ before "arrived", where does it actually come from?
quests.explanation: English avoids putting two vowel sounds directly next to each other, so speakers insert a small linking sound to bridge them. Since "crew" has no /w/ in its spelling, this /w/ is intrusive — added purely for smoothness, not because it's really part of "crew" or "arrived".
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "pass" and "your": /s/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /s/ and /j/ become /ʃ/ in "pass your" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.hint: Both "say" and "it" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "say it", an intrusive /j/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.explanation: Because "you" ends in a vowel and "owe" begins with one, English speakers instinctively insert /w/ between them. It's not in the spelling of either word — it's added on the fly to keep the speech flowing.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.explanation: Unlike linking, where the connecting sound is already written into the word, this /j/ in "okay everyone" comes from nowhere in the spelling. That's exactly what makes it intrusive rather than a genuine linking sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /s/ meets a "you"-type word. In "face your", the result is /ʃ/, not /s/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.
